coverage_analysis: The supplied batch encompasses a variety of statutory offenses under special enactments, including the Customs Act, Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, Excise Act, and Essential Commodities Act. While the existing library addresses statutory reverse-onus presumptions (LF011) and the admissibility of discovery statements leading to physical facts (LF012), it lacks a template governing the admissibility of full inculpatory statements or confessions made to special statutory officers. Three cases in the batch (il-tur-cjpe-1968_224, il-tur-cjpe-1997_1086, and il-tur-cjpe-2001_658) repeatedly demonstrate a distinct legal operation: determining that Customs and Excise officers are not 'police officers' under Section 25 of the Evidence Act because they lack the power to file a formal charge-sheet under Section 173 of the CrPC. Consequently, these cases establish that statements recorded by such officers (e.g., under Section 108 of the Customs Act) do not require the magisterial safeguards of Section 164 CrPC and are admissible as substantive evidence, provided they pass the voluntariness test under Section 24 of the Evidence Act. This constitutes a solid gap candidate.
